summary: BBN's host status report for January 17 to 28, 1972, noting that the Utah and Rand PDP-10 hosts became servers. It was replaced by RFC 306.

eli5.summary: Another report on which network computers were up in late January.

questions: when did utah and rand become servers
subtitle: ARPANET host status for January 17-28, 1972, noting Utah and Rand as new servers.

tldr.problem: ARPANET administrators needed to track host availability and know when previously unavailable hosts became functional servers.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tested hosts daily from late January 1972 and reported biweekly with detailed status tables and server predictions.
tldr.outcome: Two major sites—Utah and Rand—became PDP-10 servers, significantly expanding available computing resources on the network.

today: RFC 298 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 306. It marks an important milestone: the availability of multiple major PDP-10 servers across the ARPANET.

sections.title: Introduction and Status Updates
sections.content: RFC 298 reports on ARPANET host status from January 17 to January 28, 1972. A key note: during this period both the Utah PDP-10 and the Rand PDP-10 became network servers, a significant expansion of available computing power. The report lists hosts excluded from daily testing: those not expected to be servers for two weeks (BBN PDP-10/B, Case PDP-10, Ames and Paoli computers), and user-only hosts (Terminal IMPs, the Network Control Center, and others).
sections.eli5: A report from late January announced that two computers—one in Utah and one at Rand—could now serve other networked computers.

sections.title: Daily Test Results and Status Codes
sections.content: Two tables of daily test results span January 17-21 and January 24-28. Tests used status codes where O meant open, D meant dead, H meant half-open, R meant refused, and T meant timed out (with timeout set at 60 seconds). Sites advertising unavailable times are noted in the tables. UCLA's IBM-360 offered Remote Job Service and would offer Telnet in April. SDC remained consistently dead during this period.
sections.eli5: Tables showed which computers answered calls each day. Some computers stayed broken the whole time (SDC), while others worked most days.

sections.title: Host Server Status and Availability
sections.content: The report includes a status table with 20 hosts and their server status or predictions. Major servers like UCLA, SRI, UCSB, MIT, and Harvard show stable or improving availability. Utah and Rand PDP-10s are now marked as servers. Other hosts show mixed results: Lincoln TX2 became a server (improved from earlier reports), while Stanford and Illinois remained non-servers or unavailable. The NMC at UCLA is noted as a research site requiring prior arrangement with users.
sections.eli5: Each site said whether its computer would help others, and the tests showed which ones were already answering calls reliably.

references.text: Wentheimer, E., "Network Host Status", RFC 267, November 1971.
